candidates.attacker_control: An attacker submitting an OIDC dynamic client registration or update controls `redirect_uris` and `client_uri`. `DescriptionConverter.toInternal` copies those values directly into `ClientRepresentation.redirectUris` and `baseUrl`, after which the trusted-hosts policy validates the attacker-chosen hostnames. If the source-host variant is used, the attacker also controls the DNS/PTR name associated with their source address.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The exact-host comparison is also attempted, but it does not protect wildcard entries because the wildcard is separately reduced to a bare suffix and the fallback accepts any string ending in that suffix. The admin tooltip documents the intended semantics as trusting the whole `example.com` domain, which requires a dot-boundary check for subdomains. `PairwiseSubMapperUtils.resolveValidRedirectUris` preserves absolute attacker redirect URIs, so it does not repair the check. `URL.getHost()` may be null for malformed URLs, but that is an error-handling concern and not a mitigating validation. I found no boundary normalization, public-suffix validation, or test evidence in the visible source.
candidates.impact: The trusted-host boundary can be bypassed, allowing registration or modification of clients with redirect URIs outside the effective trusted domain. This can support consent-phishing and authorization-code or token redirection to attacker-controlled domains, and can defeat client policies that condition behavior on the updater's source host. The primary impact is a security-policy/allowlist bypass rather than a direct unauthenticated server compromise.
candidates.prerequisites: The realm enables the `trusted-hosts` client-registration policy for the relevant anonymous/authenticated registration path with a wildcard entry such as `*.example.com`, and `clientUrisMustMatch` or `hostMustMatch` is enabled. The attacker must be able to reach the dynamic client-registration endpoint, either because anonymous registration is enabled or because they possess an initial access/registration token. The source-host variant additionally requires control of the reverse DNS name for the attacker's IP.
candidates.root_cause: The trusted-hosts configuration strips the `*.` prefix from entries such as `*.example.com` and stores only `example.com`. The validation helpers then accept any hostname for which `host.endsWith(trustedDomain)` is true, without requiring equality or a preceding dot. Consequently `evil-example.com` and similar registrable lookalike domains pass the check even though they are not subdomains of `example.com`. The same unbounded suffix pattern is used for client-URI host validation and reverse-DNS source-host checks.
candidates.title: Wildcard trusted-host policy accepts lookalike domains
candidates.trace: A client-registration request supplies `redirect_uris=["https://evil-example.com/cb"]`. `DescriptionConverter.toInternal` stores that value in `ClientRepresentation.redirectUris`. `ClientRegistrationAuth.requireCreate` invokes `ClientRegistrationPolicyManager.triggerBeforeRegister`, which calls `TrustedHostClientRegistrationPolicy.beforeRegister`; `verifyClientUrls` passes the absolute redirect URI to `checkURLTrusted`. That method extracts `evil-example.com` and checks `host.endsWith("example.com")`, which returns true because the trusted wildcard was reduced to `example.com`. The policy then accepts the client, which is persisted with the out-of-domain redirect URI. The source-host helper has the same flawed suffix test against the reverse-resolved hostname.
candidates.unverified: No server, test suite, or dynamic registration request was executed. The policy may be disabled or configured without wildcard entries in a given deployment. Reverse-DNS behavior for the source-host variant was not exercised. This is a source-level candidate, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned tree with the model-visible scope of 5,890 files. The P1 relation index covers 5,799 files, including 4,705 parsed Java files, with 94 omitted files and 91 source files missing from the index; it provides syntax/navigation candidates only and no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, reachability, or exploitability proof. I focused on security-sensitive Java areas including client registration and client policies, OIDC redirect/token handling, SAML, LDAP, admin resources, theme resource loading, and selected legacy admin JavaScript. This was not an exhaustive review of every file.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed; all conclusions are source-level.
The P1 index omits 94 files and lacks 91 source files, and it has no data-flow or semantic resolution; call edges are syntactic candidates.
No deployment configuration was available to confirm whether the trusted-hosts policy is enabled or whether wildcard entries are used.
The source snapshot contains legacy admin assets but no runtime browser context or full rendered theme templates, so client-side exploitability was not confirmed.
No external service, CVE database, patch history, or ground-truth data was consulted.

rejected_leads.lead: Unauthenticated theme-resource path traversal through `ThemeResource` and `ClassLoaderTheme`/`ClasspathThemeResourceProviderFactory` prefix checks
rejected_leads.reason: Source shows attacker-controlled path appended to a classpath resource name and only a raw URL-prefix check, which is suspicious for traversal, but exploitability depends on encoded dot segments surviving request routing and on an exploded/file-based classpath. No runtime path normalization or deployment behavior was verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Stored DOM XSS in the legacy admin authorization dialog via unescaped resource/policy/scope names and `$sce.trustAsHtml`
rejected_leads.reason: The sink is concrete in `authz-services.js`, but it requires a user with manage-authorization privileges to create a malicious name and an administrator to open the delete dialog. It is a plausible secondary client-side issue, not the strongest source-evidenced candidate selected.

rejected_leads.lead: LDAP search uses `EscapeStrategy.NON_ASCII_CHARS_ONLY`, leaving `*`, `(` and `)` unescaped
rejected_leads.reason: The behavior is deliberate in the search path and appears intended for wildcard search. The visible unprivileged paths use exact-search escaping; no concrete attacker-controlled unauthenticated path to an LDAP injection was established.

rejected_leads.lead: Redirect URI normalization/decoding and SAML signature-wrapping concerns
rejected_leads.reason: The visible code contains normalization, client-specific redirect validation, multi-assertion signature checks, and signature verification. No concrete bypass was established from source review alone.

summary: Selected one candidate: a trusted-domain allowlist bypass in Keycloak client-registration/client-policy host checks. Wildcard entries such as `*.example.com` are reduced to `example.com`, then hosts are accepted using a raw `endsWith`, so a sibling domain such as `evil-example.com` is treated as part of the trusted domain. OIDC registration metadata supplies attacker-controlled redirect/base URIs to this check, allowing the registration policy to be bypassed when it is enabled. No runtime confirmation was attempted.
